Teapot Dome. The scandal that sent a Cabinet member to prison and became synonymous with government corruption during the Harding administration.

In 1921, President Harding did something secret. He transferred control of naval oil reserves from the Navy Department to the Interior Department. One reserve was at Teapot Dome, Wyoming. The other was at Elk Hills, California. These were the nation's strategic oil reserves.

Secretary of Interior Albert B. Fall then leased these reserves to oil magnates. Harry Sinclair got Mammoth Oil's contract. Edward Doheny got Pan American Petroleum's contract. There was no competitive bidding. No open process. Just backroom deals.

Fall received bribes. A lot of them. He got a ranch loan for four hundred and four thousand dollars. He received livestock and property improvements. Suddenly, he was wealthy. People noticed. He had a ranch, improvements, animals. Where did all this come from on a Cabinet officer's salary?

The scheme was exposed by Senator Thomas J. Walsh during congressional hearings in 1923 and 1924. Fall had already left office by then. Walsh was relentless in his investigation, and the truth came out.

Fall was convicted of bribery. He went to federal prison, serving nine months between 1929 and 1930. He became the first U.S. Cabinet member ever sent to prison for crimes committed in office. That was historic and humiliating.

The Supreme Court voided the oil leases. The reserves were returned to government control. But the damage to public trust was permanent. The scandal symbolized the corruption and cronyism that defined Harding's administration. It contributed to public skepticism of the federal government during the 1920s. Warren G. Harding was the president under whose watch it happened. Albert B. Fall was the Interior Secretary who orchestrated and profited from the illegal leases. Senator Thomas J. Walsh became the man whose investigations became a model for congressional oversight. And the scandal exposed the need for transparency in government contracting, a lesson America is still learning.
